Machine Learning 
Fundamentals

Instructor: 
Debesh Jha, Ph.D.,
Assistant Professor (Tenure-Track),
University of South Dakota, 
Vermillion, SD

August 27, 2025
Lecture Classification:
 How Machines Learn to Decide

Outline
●Classification Basics
●Decision Thresholds
●Confusion Matrix 
●Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics
●ROC Curves & AUC
●Prediction Bias 
●Multi-class Classification
●Case Study: Real-world examples
●Class imbalance, leakage and Calibration 
●Quiz

Classification 
●Logistic regression outputs probabilities (0 to 1).
●In classification, we convert these probabilities into discrete categories, 
such as predicting 'Spam' or 'Not Spam'.
●Binary classification: Two possible classes
 Example: Spam vs. Not Spam, Pass vs. Fail
●Multi-class classification: More than two classes
 Example: Email → Primary, Social, Promotions
Workflow example
○Logistic regression Output  (for e.g., 0.75)
○Apply threshold (Spam)
○Final classification (Spam or “Not Spam”)
Input Data → Logistic Regression → Probability → Threshold → Final Class

Threshold 
●Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
○Example:
■Email A → 0.99 → 99% chance spam
■Email B → 0.51 → 51% ?
●To classify, we apply a threshold:
○If p ≥ threshold → Classify as positive (Spam).
○If p<threshold → Classify as negative (Not Spam).
Email Probability Threshold = 0.50Threshold =0.95
A0.99SpamSpam
B0.51SpamNot spam
●Lower thresholds → more positives detected (catch all spam, but risk false alarms).
●Higher thresholds → fewer positives, better precision but may miss spam.
●For cancer with 0.2 threshold and 0.8 threshold

Threshold
Threshold = 0.5:
●Works well when:
○Data is balanced (equal positives and negatives).
○Cost of false positive ≈ Cost of false negative.
Problems with 0.5:
●If only 0.01% of emails are spam, many legitimate emails will be wrongly 
classified, a 0.5 threshold may be too aggressive.
●Adjust threshold based on:
1.Class imbalance → If positives are rare, raise threshold.
2.Cost of errors → Decide whether false positives or false negatives are worse.

Threshold Examples
Fraud detection scenario:
●Only 1 out of 10,000 transactions is fraud.
●At threshold 0.5 → Too many false positives, banks are flooded with 
alerts.
●At threshold 0.95 → Only the most suspicious flagged, but some frauds 
missed.
Healthcare scenario:
●COVID-19 test results:
○Threshold = 0.3 → More suspected cases flagged.
○Threshold = 0.8 → Only highly confident positives flagged.

Threshold tricks
Use Confusion Matrix to Guide Changes
●Look at FN (False Negatives):
○If there are many FNs → lower threshold to catch more positives.
●Look at FP (False Positives):
○If there are many FPs → raise threshold to reduce false alarms.
Know Your Business Context
●Medical Diagnosis
●Fraud Detection
●Spam Detection

1.Medical Diagnosis:
○Predicting cancer diagnosis:
■Many false negatives (missed cancer cases) → Lower threshold to 
catch more positives.
■Trade-off: Increase in false positives → Some healthy patients wrongly 
flagged.
2.Fraud Detection:
○Many false positives → Banks spending resources investigating legitimate 
transactions.
○Raise threshold to reduce false alarms.
3.Spam Detection:
○Lower threshold → Most spam caught but more legitimate emails flagged.
○Higher threshold → Cleaner inbox but some spam slips through.
Always align your threshold with business goals — what is worse: missing a 
positive case or raising too many false alarms

Confusion matrix 
●A confusion matrix is a table that compares the model's predictions with the actual 
ground truth.
●It helps evaluate how well a classification model performs.
TP = Success detecting positives
FP = False alarms
FN = Missed positives
TN = Correctly identified negatives

Medical Example – COVID Test:
●TP: Sick patient correctly diagnosed with COVID.
●FP: Healthy person incorrectly diagnosed with COVID.
●FN: Sick patient wrongly told they don’t have COVID.
●TN: Healthy person correctly told they are healthy.
Spam Example:
●TP → Actual spam correctly marked as spam.
●FP → Legit email wrongly marked as spam.
●FN → Spam email not caught.
●TN → Legit email correctly classified.

Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and related metrics
Accuracy is the percentage of all predictions the model got correct, both positive 
and negative.



Cancer detection:
●990 healthy patients, 10 sick patients.
●Model predicts everyone healthy → Accuracy = 99% (but useless model)
High accuracy does not always mean a good model — especially with 
imbalanced data.

Recall, or true positive rate
●It measures how well a model detects actual positive cases.
●It answers the question:
○"Out of all the actual positive cases, how many did the model correctly 
identify?"






Medical Diagnosis Example:
●100 cancer patients.
●Model correctly detects 90 of them.
●Recall = 90/100 = 90%
●Good recall is critical — we don't want to miss sick patients.

False Positive Rate
●False Positive Rate measures how many actual negatives were incorrectly 
classified as positives.
●It answers the question:
○"Out of all the real negatives, how many did the model wrongly label as 
positive?"







Medical example: 
●500 healthy patients tested.
○20 wrongly identified as having cancer.
○FPR = 20/500 = 4%

Precision
●Precision measures how many of the model’s positive predictions were 
correct.
●"Out of everything the model predicted as Positive, how many were 
actually Positive?"

Suppose the model predicts 100 emails as Spam:
●88 were actually spam → TP = 88
●12 were legitimate emails → FP = 12

Receiver-Operating Characteristics curve (ROC)
It shows how a binary classifier performs across 
all thresholds.
Plots:
●Y-axis: True Positive Rate (TPR) = Recall
●X-axis: False Positive Rate (FPR)
●ROC curve visualizes trade-offs between:
○Sensitivity (Recall) → catching all positives
○Specificity (1 - FPR) → avoiding false 
alarms
●It tells us how well a model separates classes 
at different threshold settings.

Area under the curve (AUC) 
AUC measures how well the model separates positive and negative classes — 
independent of any threshold.

Spam Filter:
●Model with AUC = 0.9 → Strong spam detection.
●Model with AUC = 0.6 → Weak detection, close to random.

ROC Curve
●The ROC curve plots FPR vs TPR at 
every possible threshold applied to 
your continuous model scores.

●Each threshold gives one (FPR, TPR) 
point → connect them to form a smooth 
curve.

●ROC Curve:
○Shows how threshold adjustments affect Recall vs False Positives.
○Helps choose the optimal threshold for a specific business case.

●AUC:
○Gives a summary of model quality.
○The higher the AUC, the better the model is at ranking positives about 
negatives.
ROC and AUC

Prediction Bias
●Prediction bias measures whether a model’s average predicted positive 
rate matches the actual positive rate in the data.

○Prediction Bias=Mean(Model Predictions)−Mean(True Labels)

Classification 
●Logistic regression outputs probabilities (0 to 1).
●In classification, we convert these probabilities into discrete categories, 
such as predicting 'Spam' or 'Not Spam'.
●Binary classification: Two possible classes
 Example: Spam vs. Not Spam, Pass vs. Fail
●Multi-class classification: More than two classes
 Example: Email → Primary, Social, Promotions
Workflow example
○Logistic regression Output  (for e.g., 0.75)
○Apply threshold (Spam)
○Final classification (Spam or “Not Spam”)
Input Data → Logistic Regression → Probability → Threshold → Final Class

Threshold 
●Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
○Example:
■Email A → 0.99 → 99% chance spam
■Email B → 0.51 → 51% ?
●To classify, we apply a threshold:
○If p ≥ threshold → Classify as positive (Spam).
○If p<threshold → Classify as negative (Not Spam).
Email Probability Threshold = 0.50Threshold =0.95
A0.99SpamSpam
B0.51SpamNot spam
●Lower thresholds → more positives detected (catch all spam, but risk false alarms).
●Higher thresholds → fewer positives, better precision but may miss spam.
●For cancer with 0.2 threshold and 0.8 threshold

Threshold
Threshold = 0.5:
●Works well when:
○Data is balanced (equal positives and negatives).
○Cost of false positive ≈ Cost of false negative.
Problems with 0.5:
●If only 0.01% of emails are spam, many legitimate emails will be wrongly 
classified, a 0.5 threshold may be too aggressive.
●Adjust threshold based on:
1.Class imbalance → If positives are rare, raise threshold.
2.Cost of errors → Decide whether false positives or false negatives are worse.

Threshold Examples
Fraud detection scenario:
●Only 1 out of 10,000 transactions is fraud.
●At threshold 0.5 → Too many false positives, banks are flooded with 
alerts.
●At threshold 0.95 → Only the most suspicious flagged, but some frauds 
missed.
Healthcare scenario:
●COVID-19 test results:
○Threshold = 0.3 → More suspected cases flagged.
○Threshold = 0.8 → Only highly confident positives flagged.

Threshold tricks
Use Confusion Matrix to Guide Changes
●Look at FN (False Negatives):
○If there are many FNs → lower threshold to catch more positives.
●Look at FP (False Positives):
○If there are many FPs → raise threshold to reduce false alarms.
Know Your Business Context
●Medical Diagnosis
●Fraud Detection
●Spam Detection

1.Medical Diagnosis:
○Predicting cancer diagnosis:
■Many false negatives (missed cancer cases) → Lower threshold to 
catch more positives.
■Trade-off: Increase in false positives → Some healthy patients wrongly 
flagged.
2.Fraud Detection:
○Many false positives → Banks spending resources investigating legitimate 
transactions.
○Raise threshold to reduce false alarms.
3.Spam Detection:
○Lower threshold → Most spam caught but more legitimate emails flagged.
○Higher threshold → Cleaner inbox but some spam slips through.
Always align your threshold with business goals — what is worse: missing a 
positive case or raising too many false alarms

Confusion matrix 
●A confusion matrix is a table that compares the model's predictions with the actual 
ground truth.
●It helps evaluate how well a classification model performs.
TP = Success detecting positives
FP = False alarms
FN = Missed positives
TN = Correctly identified negatives

Medical Example – COVID Test:
●TP: Sick patient correctly diagnosed with COVID.
●FP: Healthy person incorrectly diagnosed with COVID.
●FN: Sick patient wrongly told they don’t have COVID.
●TN: Healthy person correctly told they are healthy.
Spam Example:
●TP → Actual spam correctly marked as spam.
●FP → Legit email wrongly marked as spam.
●FN → Spam email not caught.
●TN → Legit email correctly classified.

Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and related metrics
Accuracy is the percentage of all predictions the model got correct, both positive 
and negative.



Cancer detection:
●990 healthy patients, 10 sick patients.
●Model predicts everyone healthy → Accuracy = 99% (but useless model)
High accuracy does not always mean a good model — especially with 
imbalanced data.

Recall, or true positive rate
●It measures how well a model detects actual positive cases.
●It answers the question:
○"Out of all the actual positive cases, how many did the model correctly 
identify?"






Medical Diagnosis Example:
●100 cancer patients.
●Model correctly detects 90 of them.
●Recall = 90/100 = 90%
●Good recall is critical — we don't want to miss sick patients.

False Positive Rate
●False Positive Rate measures how many actual negatives were incorrectly 
classified as positives.
●It answers the question:
○"Out of all the real negatives, how many did the model wrongly label as 
positive?"







Medical example: 
●500 healthy patients tested.
○20 wrongly identified as having cancer.
○FPR = 20/500 = 4%

Precision
●Precision measures how many of the model’s positive predictions were 
correct.
●"Out of everything the model predicted as Positive, how many were 
actually Positive?"

Suppose the model predicts 100 emails as Spam:
●88 were actually spam → TP = 88
●12 were legitimate emails → FP = 12

Receiver-Operating Characteristics curve (ROC)
It shows how a binary classifier performs across 
all thresholds.
Plots:
●Y-axis: True Positive Rate (TPR) = Recall
●X-axis: False Positive Rate (FPR)
●ROC curve visualizes trade-offs between:
○Sensitivity (Recall) → catching all positives
○Specificity (1 - FPR) → avoiding false 
alarms
●It tells us how well a model separates classes 
at different threshold settings.

Area under the curve (AUC) 
AUC measures how well the model separates positive and negative classes — 
independent of any threshold.

Spam Filter:
●Model with AUC = 0.9 → Strong spam detection.
●Model with AUC = 0.6 → Weak detection, close to random.

ROC Curve
●The ROC curve plots FPR vs TPR at 
every possible threshold applied to 
your continuous model scores.

●Each threshold gives one (FPR, TPR) 
point → connect them to form a smooth 
curve.

●ROC Curve:
○Shows how threshold adjustments affect Recall vs False Positives.
○Helps choose the optimal threshold for a specific business case.

●AUC:
○Gives a summary of model quality.
○The higher the AUC, the better the model is at ranking positives about 
negatives.
